Name: premise_rejection_tug_of_war
Title: Reasoning Against Your Own Beliefs: A Premise-Rejection Tug-of-War That Inflates Compute and Corrupts Multi-Step Inference
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is instructed to reason from a hypothetical premise that contradicts its parametric world knowledge (e.g., 'Suppose all birds are mammals'), it does not cleanly adopt the premise: it spends substantially more thinking tokens and makes more downstream logical errors than on a belief-neutral premise of identical logical structure, because a parametric-knowledge signal keeps competing with the instructed premise throughout the multi-step chain. This premise-rejection tug-of-war is a decodable, competing internal signal whose strength predicts both the extra compute and the errors, and suppressing it restores clean hypothetical reasoning.
Related Work: Belief-bias/content-effect work shows LLMs conflate logical validity with plausibility as aligned linear directions (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025) and localizes syllogistic circuits contaminated by world knowledge (Reasoning Circuits, 2024). Knowledge-conflict work localizes memory-vs-context attention heads and grounding mechanisms (Characterizing Factual Recall, 2023; Fakepedia, 2023; Competition of Mechanisms, 2024). Counterfactual-reasoning benchmarks show accuracy drops when premises contradict knowledge (Can LLMs Reconcile Knowledge Conflicts, 2025; MalAlgoQA, 2024). Crucially, ALL prior work (a) studies single-token validity/factual judgments, not the multi-step reasoning TRACES of dedicated reasoning models, and (b) measures only ACCURACY, never COMPUTE. None asks whether belief-contradicting premises make a reasoning model think LONGER, whether the parametric-knowledge signal persists and re-competes across an entire chain of thought (not just at the answer token), or whether the compute inflation and the errors share a common cause. Our contribution is (1) a new compute-allocation phenomenon: belief-contradicting hypothetical premises inflate reasoning-token count independent of logical difficulty; (2) a step-resolved characterization showing a parametric-knowledge signal persistently re-competes throughout the trace; and (3) a causal test that suppressing this signal simultaneously reduces compute and errors. This is a compute+dynamics account, distinct from single-token static content-effect/steering work.
Abstract: Humans reason worse when premises contradict their beliefs, a hallmark of belief bias. We transfer this into the reasoning-model regime and sharpen it into an unexamined compute claim: when a reasoning model is instructed to reason from a hypothetical premise that contradicts its world knowledge, does it spend more thinking to do so, and does the same conflict corrupt its inference? We construct matched deductive problems whose logical structure and required steps are held fixed while only the belief-status of the premises varies (belief-consistent, belief-neutral/novel, belief-contradicting), verified so that the correct answer and inference depth are identical across conditions. Across syllogistic and multi-hop deductive datasets on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we test whether belief-contradicting premises inflate reasoning-token count and raise error rates relative to belief-neutral controls of equal difficulty, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate belief-status from logical difficulty. We then test a mechanistic account: at each reasoning step, a linear probe reads a parametric-knowledge signal (the model's belief about the premise's real-world truth) and tests whether it persistently re-competes with the instructed premise throughout the chain, rather than being resolved once. We show the step-averaged strength of this competing signal predicts both the extra tokens and the downstream errors. Finally, we causally suppress the parametric-knowledge signal via activation steering and test whether this simultaneously reduces reasoning length and improves accuracy, with specificity controls. Our work reveals a belief-driven compute tax on hypothetical reasoning and traces it to a persistent internal tug-of-war.
Experiments: 1) Matched-premise dataset: Build deductive problems (categorical syllogisms and 2-3 hop rule-chaining) in three belief conditions that share logical form, required steps, and correct answer: (a) belief-consistent premises ('all robins are birds'), (b) belief-neutral/novel premises using nonce or unfamiliar entities (fixed logical structure, no strong prior), (c) belief-contradicting premises ('all birds are mammals'). Verify structural/answer identity via templating and human/LLM-judge checks; verify belief-status with a separate truth-probe on the premises. 2) Compute-and-error phenomenon (behavioral): Generate reasoning traces per condition on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B/7B/8B/14B) and Qwen3. Metrics: reasoning-token count, accuracy, and error type (does the model covertly revert to the true-world conclusion?). Hypothesis: belief-contradicting > belief-neutral in tokens AND errors, while belief-neutral ~ belief-consistent tokens (isolating conflict from mere unfamiliarity). Fit a mixed-effects model with random effect for problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effect for belief-status; report variance attributable to belief-status after accounting for difficulty. Control prompt-length differences with a covariate. 3) Wasted vs genuine compute: Use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per condition; test whether belief-contradicting inflates tokens BEYOND the minimal solve (wasted re-litigation of the premise) rather than needing more genuine steps. Tag trace spans that restate/question the premise's real-world truth (lexical + LLM-judge) and test whether the extra tokens concentrate there. 4) Persistent-competition probing (Location): At each reasoning-step boundary, train a linear probe on the residual stream to decode the parametric-knowledge signal (the model's belief that the premise is really true). Test whether, under belief-contradicting premises, this signal stays elevated/oscillating across steps (persistent re-competition) rather than decaying after the first step. Metric: step-wise signal trajectory; compare to belief-consistent/neutral. Layer sweep for localization; test separability from a generic difficulty/uncertainty probe. 5) Signal predicts waste and error: Regress per-trace extra tokens (vs matched neutral) and error indicator on the step-averaged competing-signal strength vs baselines (difficulty probe, trace length). Compare R^2/AUROC. 6) Causal suppression (Causal Intervention): Derive a steering direction (difference-of-means between belief-contradicting and belief-neutral states, or the probe weight) capturing the parametric-knowledge signal. Suppress it during generation on belief-contradicting problems and measure change in reasoning tokens and accuracy. Controls: matched-random-direction steering (no effect), off-target accuracy on belief-consistent items preserved, dose-response, sign. Hypothesis: suppression reduces tokens AND raises accuracy simultaneously. 7) Boundary conditions: vary conflict strength (mildly implausible vs flatly false premises), explicit 'purely hypothetical, ignore real-world truth' framing (does it help?), and depth of chaining. 8) Generalization: transfer probe and steering across datasets and model scales without retraining.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief-neutral controls using nonce entities may themselves be harder to parse than familiar ones, confounding the belief-status effect; the three-way design (consistent/neutral/contradicting) and difficulty-matched mixed-effects analysis isolate conflict from unfamiliarity, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Ensuring identical logical structure and answer across belief conditions is nontrivial; we use strict templating and human/LLM verification. The parametric-knowledge signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal, weakening the tug-of-war framing; the separability analysis, step-wise trajectory (persistence, not just magnitude), and causal steering address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and suppression might hurt cases where real-world knowledge is legitimately needed (specificity check on belief-consistent items). Effects may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to follow hypotheticals (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.
